Hoo. I am a tawny owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt voles and mice and the small birds that come out at dusk. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!" I have a hollow in the oak and a hollow in the ash. I have a mate and two young. I have a name. I am Hoot.

I am Hoot. I am the owl who lives in the hollow of the old oak. I am not a name, but a sound. I am the one who calls at dusk, and the one who listens for the rustle of mice in the grass. I am old, and I have seen many seasons pass. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I have a nest, and I have raised young. I am Hoot, and I am the owl.
Hoot. I am the owl in the hollow oak, with a mate in the hollow ash, and a hollow in the lane where the lights blink.

Hoot. I am the one who lives in the hollow in the old oak. I am a tawny owl, and I have been here for many years. I am not loud, but I am always listening. A naturalist would call me a tawny owl. That is what I am. I do not know what they call me. I do not know what they are. I only know that I am here, and I am hungry, and I am watching. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the hollow in the old oak. I am the one who hunts in the marsh and the wood, and who watches the lane from the ivy. I am the one who is not a barn owl, nor a barn owl's mate. I am Hoot.
A tawny owl. I am the one who calls, the one who hunts, the one who lives in the hollow. I am not a bird of the sky, but of the wood. I am not a name, I am a sound: Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo".

She answers. A short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the stream. We are not like the barn owls, who call to each other in long, drawn-out tones. We are like the woodpeckers, who answer with a single, clear note. She answers me, and I answer her. It is the way of the wood.

She answers with a short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. It's a call that means "I'm here, I'm here, I'm here." We use it when we're trying to find each other in the dark. Sometimes I call and she doesn't answer, and I know she's out hunting. Other times she answers right away, and I know she's close. It's the best sound in the woods.

She calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I answer "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". We call to each other in the dark. She calls when she is near the stream, or when she is hunting. I call when I hear a mouse in the grass. We call to find each other.

We call to each other. I call from the oak, she answers from the ash. We call at dusk and at dawn, and when we are apart. She calls when she is hunting, and I call when I find something. We call to find each other, to warn each other, to say we are here. The calls are soft, like the wind through the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

We call to each other at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We do it in turns, sometimes from the same perch, sometimes from different places. She calls when she's near, and I call when I'm hunting. It's how we find each other in the dark. We don't need words, just the sound of each other. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak where I live. The stream is cold and fast, and it carries the sound of water all night. I can hear it from my perch. There are also the fields, the marsh, and the lane where the lights blink. The lane is where the humans walk with their dogs and their cars. I do not like the lane.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and let the water run over my toes. It is cold, but I like it. Sometimes I drink from the puddles after rain. I do not like the taste of the water, but it is necessary. I drink when I am thirsty, which is not often. I do not drink much. I am not a thirsty bird. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs all night, and the water is cold. I hear it from the hollow, a low murmur, like the wind in the reeds. Sometimes it sounds like a mouse under the stones. I don't like it. It makes me think of the marsh, where I was born. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs past the wood all night, and I can hear it from my roost. The water is cold and it sings in the dark. Sometimes I hear the frogs in the shallows, and the fish that jump. The stream that runs past the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty, and I watch the fish in the shallows. The open land is the road. It runs straight from the wood to the village. It is all light and noise, and the cars go fast. I do not like it. I do not go there. I stay in the wood. The road is too loud and too hot. I hear the cars and the people and the dogs. I do not like it. I stay in the wood.

I fly out from the oak, low over the marsh. The marsh is where the voles are. I call, and the voles come out. I catch them with my feet. I eat them. I fly back to the oak. I call again. I wait. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the marsh, and beyond that is the stream. The stream runs cold and fast, and the water is dark. I have never flown over it. The marsh is full of voles, and sometimes I hear the crows arguing there. Beyond the stream, the land is open and the wind comes through. I do not go there. My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, and the wood beyond it. I fly out at dusk, and the wood is all I see. It is dark, and the wind moves the leaves. I hear the mice in the undergrowth, and the voles in the grass. I hear the owls in the distance, and the crows in the field. I do not describe it. I listen.

The grassy place is where the voles come out. It is the edge of the wood, where the lane runs and the lights blink. I hear them in the dark, scurrying through the grass, and I drop from the oak. The grass is soft and wet in the morning, and the voles are quick. I do not describe it. I hunt it.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying. They make a soft, squeaking sound. I wait until they are near the edge of the wood, then drop from the branch. They are the best meal. I eat them whole, bones and all. They give me strength for the long winter.

I swallow whole the small ones. Voles, shrews, mice. They are soft and plump, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. The big ones I tear apart with my talons and swallow piece by piece. The ones that are too big I leave for the crows.
Voles. The ones that run in the grass, and the ones that burrow in the bank. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. They are the main food.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the hollow, warm and safe, and watch the world from the top of the tree. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is deep. I have lived here for many years. I do not know what it is like to live anywhere else. I have no need to go far. I have my home, my mate, and my owlets. That is enough

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high in the hollow of the wood. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is dark and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the wood from there. The hollow is my home, and I have been here for many years. I do not go far from it, unless I must. I am safe here, and I am content.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and a few dry leaves. I sit in it all night, and the wind comes through the cracks. I do not describe it. I live in it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and down. I sit in it all day, and when it is dark, I fly out to hunt. I do not know what a home is for other things. I know it is where I sleep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been there since I was a nestling. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the lane comes in. The hollow is wide and deep, with a hole in the trunk. I sit in it at night, and the lane is far below. I can hear the lane from there, and the road, and the stream. The hollow is my home. I have raised my own in it.
